title: Why AI Washing Won’t Work Much Longer
dek: Palantir posts an 'otherworldly' quarter while Alex Karp torches the 'token industrial complex' — and a new open-weights Qwen release lands just as a former Lululemon CIO calls time on AI wishing and washing. The thread connecting it all: the enterprise is finally asking sophisticated enough questions that faking it is about to stop paying.

oneIdea.headline: AI washing won't work much longer — the enterprise is getting too sophisticated to fool.
oneIdea.summary: A year ago enterprises were counting their first AI use cases; now they're debating open-weights policies, fine-tuning strategies, cost provisioning, and routers. That shift is why a release like Qwen 3.8 Max suddenly matters to enterprise IT, not just early adopters — and it's why the PR-driven era of AI wishing and washing that Lululemon's former CIO describes is running out of road. As the board-pleasing shortcuts stop paying, the incentive loop to do AI the wrong way gets cut off, and the real work of redesigning around AI can begin.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: "AI wishing" has an NHS accent, and it sounds like a pilot
items.body: Julie Averill's phrase for waving AI at a hard problem and skipping the work of solving it will be familiar to anyone who has sat through a transformation meeting. In general practice it usually arrives as a pilot: a tool is procured, a few enthusiasts use it, a slide says the backlog will fall, and nobody redesigns the appointment book, the admin workflow or the roles around it. Her sharper point is the one to carry into any ICB conversation — this kind of work does not happen in a quarter, and believing that it can is the trap. NHS planning runs on quarters and annual returns, so the incentive to declare success early is stronger here than in most industries, not weaker.

items.title: The layoff-and-rehire cycle is the warning worth borrowing
items.body: The figure in this edition that should travel is the survey finding that around a third of hiring managers who cut a role citing AI had already rehired for the same or a similar post. Primary care is not going to make redundancies over a scribe, but the same logic reaches us as vacancy control and skill-mix: leaving a post unfilled because a system is coming, or thinning reception and coding staff on the assumption that automation will absorb the work. Real efficiency shows up first as measurable time released — minutes per consultation, letters turned round, coding queries cleared — and only afterwards, if at all, in headcount. Reversing an establishment decision costs far more than making it, and the people asked to stay pay for it in goodwill.

items.title: If Zitron is right the price rises; if NLW is right the choice widens — either way, ask about exit
items.body: Zitron's case is that demand outside the labs is thin and today's prices are a subsidy that must eventually be withdrawn. NLW's is that the market is broadening — a two-point-four-trillion-parameter open-weights model priced at a fifth of the frontier is now something enterprise IT actually notices. A practice cannot arbitrate that, but both readings point the same way for procurement. Do not sign anything whose value depends on current per-seat pricing holding, and treat conspicuously cheap AI as a commercial risk to record rather than a bargain. The questions stay dull: what is the notice period, where does the data sit, and can we export the record in a usable form. Note also the DNA-database item — 1995-vintage software running critical evidence with no tamper detection is not a distant problem when you consider how much NHS clinical software is of similar vintage.

the_other_side.text: NLW's lead is that enterprise demand has grown up — buyers now argue about open-weights policy, routers and cost provisioning rather than counting their first two use cases — and that this new sophistication is what will finally kill AI washing. Zitron, publishing the same day, argues that the demand being celebrated is largely manufactured. Citing Barclays estimates, he puts OpenAI's and Anthropic's compute spend at around 73% of Amazon's AI revenues, and points to Wells Fargo's figure of roughly $3.9bn for Microsoft 365 Copilot across some 30 million paid seats — a per-seat number he reads as heavy discounting rather than pull. His conclusion is blunt: "the demand for AI-powered software is not there," and hyperscaler growth is mostly the big three funding their own largest customers in a circle.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men orbit one variable: whether AI revenue from ordinary buyers — firms that are neither a frontier lab nor a lab's backer — is real and compounding. They agree on more than the tone suggests: that capex is enormous, that the labs' own compute spend is a large share of reported AI revenue, and that much announced enterprise AI is theatre. The empirical question is customer concentration, and the observable that settles it is a hyperscaler disclosing AI revenue net of OpenAI and Anthropic compute spend, alongside revenue per paid seat for embedded AI software. The residue is worldview: whether sophisticated procurement questions show real adoption or a better-dressed purchasing ritual. NLW is vindicated if non-lab AI software revenue grows materially; Zitron if that figure stays in the low tens of billions against a trillion in capex. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both now call the cost-cutting AI story a fiction. Watch whether any hyperscaler breaks out AI revenue by customer next quarter.

headlines.headline: Palantir's 'otherworldly' quarter says enterprise AI demand is still booming
headlines.summary: Quarterly revenue hit $1.94 billion, up 93% year over year, with commercial sales up 149% — accelerating from 133% growth in Q1. Net income reached $1 billion, growing at a 225% annual pace, and the hiked annual forecast sent the stock up 10% after hours. NLW's aside on the token-budget headlines: caps, which most organizations haven't come close to hitting, are not the same as cuts.

headlines.headline: We do not get paid for clicks or tokens or chats.
headlines.summary: Karp's shareholder letter frames Palantir's results as demand for AI sovereignty — and paints the frontier labs as 'structurally designed' to capture their customers' organizational alpha. He even claims 'Marxist overtones' to the business, accusing model builders of trying to capture the means of production of their purported partners, and says Palantir declines 'parasitic' relationships. His name for the enemy: the 'token industrial complex.'

headlines.headline: We have people trying to drug addict us to a future they believe they control.
headlines.attribution: Alex Karp, Palantir CEO, on CNBC
headlines.summary: In a follow-up CNBC interview, Karp named names: 'I've spent a lot of time with Dario and the effective altruism crew. They wanna tell you we have to march into a future where we own nothing, where your businesses aren't profitable, where none of us have jobs, and where our adversaries win.' Not everyone took it at face value — Amit is investing offered the optimistic read: the age of AI is about empowering workers and growing GDP, not valuations.

headlines.headline: OpenAI bites back at Apple — and drops a jaw-dropper
headlines.summary: In the trade-secrets lawsuit over a departed Apple employee, OpenAI's letter calls the suit 'careless, aggressive, and oddly personal.' The wild detail: Apple claimed it contacted OpenAI in February and got no response — but per OpenAI, Apple's outside lawyers had emailed the wrong person after confusing two Asian last names, admitting it only when OpenAI pointed it out. Mostly psychodrama for now, but worth watching if it shifts OpenAI's hardware plans.

headlines.headline: The biggest scientific bet civilization has ever made.
headlines.attribution: Jasjeet Sekhon, Google DeepMind chief strategy officer
headlines.summary: At a UC Berkeley panel, DeepMind's chief strategy officer reframed sky-high CapEx as a down payment on recursive self-improvement. He acknowledged current AI revenues 'don't sustain the capital expenditures we're making so far,' creating a 'danger we could hit an AI air pocket' — but argued the build-out isn't about near-term revenue at all.

headlines.headline: Claude helps expose a decades-old hole in DNA evidence databases
headlines.summary: Researchers found they could alter forensic DNA files using Claude-written code in about 45 minutes — the database software dates to 1995 and lacks modern tamper-evident protections, with some encryption relying on a key that's been on the internet for years. No tampering has been reported, but labs also have no way to detect if it occurred; the software's creator has since pushed digital signatures with CISA's help.

headlines.headline: AI is a massive upgrade for cyber defenders, not just criminals
headlines.summary: Hundreds or thousands of outdated systems like the DNA database run critical infrastructure, and cost is the biggest reason they've never been properly tested. The ability to do even rudimentary vulnerability testing with AI on a modest budget could be a game changer — the scary-tools headline cuts both ways.

headlines.headline: White House convenes AI companies on voluntary frontier review
headlines.summary: The administration is hosting a set of AI companies to discuss its voluntary review framework for frontier models. NLW is holding off until there's solid reporting — expect a follow-up.

headlines.headline: In one year, the enterprise AI conversation grew up
headlines.summary: At KPMG's 2025 symposium, the talk was about whether organizations had one, two, or three AI use cases. This year: governance for ubiquitous coding tools, cost provisioning across models and business units, and whether to have an open-weights model policy. The quality of the questions enterprises are asking has increased dramatically — which means enterprise IT buyers, not just early-adopter developers, now pay attention to releases like Qwen 3.8 Max.

headlines.headline: Qwen 3.8 Max: 2.4 trillion parameters and 10+ days of autonomous coding
headlines.summary: Alibaba's new model would have been the top open model in the world but for the recent Kimi K3 release, per Latent Space. The Qwen team calls it 'a new bar for coding and co-work,' pointing to ten-plus days of self-evolving development from empty folder to production without hand-holding, with a complete project trace shared on GitHub.

headlines.headline: Self-reported benchmarks put Qwen between the frontier flagships
headlines.summary: Alibaba reports terminal bench and co-work bench scores between Fable 5 and GPT-6-Soul, state-of-the-art visual reasoning and research reproduction, and — most significant if accurate — state-of-the-art on OS World Verified, the agentic computer-use benchmark that matters most for agentic work applicability.

headlines.headline: The computers are going to do our jobs for us, and we're all going to the beach.
headlines.summary: Qwen's launch ad — a laptop doing coding, science, and knowledge work while its humans fish, play tennis, rock climb, and read — dominated the discourse. Calacanis called it 'world positive AI marketing' from China; Nansen's Alex Svanevik quipped, 'What is this marketing? No graveyards? No entry-level jobs disappearing?'

headlines.headline: Qwen goes back to open weights — at Max scale for the first time
headlines.summary: After last year's move from open to closed for its largest Max-series models raised questions about whether frontier-adjacent Chinese models would all close up, Alibaba is reversing course: this is the first open-sourced Qwen Max-class model, with full weights due next week. Strawberry Labs' Chirag Asarpotra: 'Chinese labs are clearly taking advantage of Anthropic's recent PR mess and are going all in on open weights. The message is loud. They want Chinese open models to dominate globally.'

headlines.headline: Qwen resets the price curve — but kills the pennies-on-the-dollar myth first
headlines.summary: Policy folks still assume every Chinese model costs cents on the dollar; in reality Kimi K3 is only about 40% cheaper than Opus ($15 vs $25 per million output tokens). Qwen 3.8 Max, though, comes in at $2 per million input and $6 per million output — roughly a third of Kimi's price and a fifth of Opus's.

headlines.headline: Early independent testing says: hold the hype
headlines.summary: Artificial Analysis published a score of 53 — four points behind Kimi K3 and a point behind Grok 4.5 — then took it down without explanation. Ethan Mollick found it 'solid but not Kimi K3 level'; Datam called it 'unusable,' last in every head-to-head. On Pavel Hurin's Bug Bench, Qwen found 19 of 105 hidden bugs at ~$31 in cost and constant friction, while GPT 5.6 Luna fixed 33 for $1.80.

headlines.headline: Why a mid-tier benchmark score doesn't kill the excitement
headlines.summary: Open weights mean people can get their hands on the model in a totally different way. And a release that in the past only developers and early adopters would notice is now on the radar of folks inside big mainstream enterprises — that's the real shift.

headlines.headline: 'AI wishing': the belief that AI is a magic wand
headlines.summary: In a New York Times op-ed, former Lululemon CIO Julie Averill coins 'AI wishing' — leaders believing you can wave AI at a hard problem and skip the work of solving it. It's not a critique of AI, which she calls the most powerful technology she's seen, already remaking pharma, banking, and national security — it's a critique of the human processes around how AI gets integrated.

headlines.headline: This kind of work doesn't happen in a quarter, and believing that it can is the trap.
headlines.attribution: Julie Averill, former Lululemon CIO, in The New York Times
headlines.summary: The most important line in the piece: real AI transformation — the kind rebuilding drug discovery and fraud detection — takes sustained work, and quarterly-results thinking is exactly what produces AI wishing's 'insidious cousin,' AI washing.

headlines.headline: The AI layoff is often a cash grab wearing an efficiency costume
headlines.summary: Averill's most damning example: companies claim AI made them efficient enough to cut jobs when the efficiency doesn't exist yet — the cut frees up cash, sometimes to spend on AI. In May, US employers announced 97,000 job cuts and blamed 40% on AI; a separate survey found a third of hiring managers who cut a role for AI had already rehired for the same or similar one. The cycle burns money, talent, and the trust of everyone asked to stay.

headlines.headline: Efficiency-only AI companies will get pummeled by opportunity companies
headlines.summary: Organizations that view AI strictly as an efficiency technology might eke out a few headline wins, but they'll ultimately be beaten by companies that understand this is a redesign moment — organizational, job-role, and process redesign — not a chance to excite shareholders about Q3 cost cuts. Shortcuts are bound to fail.

headlines.headline: Open-weights policies and routers are becoming real enterprise disciplines
headlines.summary: A year ago almost no company had an expressed open-weights policy beyond 'no Chinese models.' Now there are Forbes op-eds urging leaders to learn them, Thinking Machines Lab's Tinker offers fine-tuning, Microsoft is building a frontier tuning service on its lower-cost MAI models, and reports say Stripe is about to buy OpenRouter for $10 billion. As one recent post put it: 'AI cost optimization is now a discipline, not a hack.'

headlines.headline: For the first time since ChatGPT, enterprise conventional wisdom is getting directionally correct
headlines.summary: The hills are still steep for opportunity-AI advocates inside their organizations. But attitudes toward AI wishing and washing are changing radically, the PR value and board plaudits are drying up — and that helpfully cuts off the incentive loop to do AI the wrong way, leaving the exciting work of actually redesigning around AI's capabilities.
